own_solution.law: For a stationary incline, conservation of mechanical energy gives (1/2)mv0² + (1/2)(2mR²/5)(v0/R)² = mgd sinθ, hence d = 7v0²/(10g sinθ). The deceleration magnitude is 5g sinθ/7.
assumptions: The sphere rolls without slipping throughout its ascent.
The incline is stationary at the specified angle throughout the ascent.
Air resistance and rolling resistance are negligible.
Static friction does no work on the stationary incline.

TD438.regime: A stationary incline permits pure rolling when μs ≥ (2/7)tan25° ≈ 0.13323; all listed coefficients satisfy this.

T1F4F.regime: A stationary incline permits pure rolling when μs ≥ (2/7)tan25° ≈ 0.13323; all listed coefficients satisfy this.

uncertain_fields: Whether the stated 25-degree angle precedes or follows the prelaunch adjustment in TDEF6.
The timing, pivot and motion of the incline adjustment in T96D5.

defect_reasons.insufficient_boundary_condition: T96D5 does not establish that the adjustment finishes before launch or specify the support motion if it occurs during the ascent, so replacing θ by θ + q does not determine a unique answer.
defect_reasons.missing_assumption: The authors' outside-regime reference expression uses the static friction coefficient as the sliding friction coefficient without specifying a kinetic friction law or assuming equality of the two coefficients.

counterexamples.description: Completing the adjustment before the specified 6 m/s launch gives 4.17669 m at 38 degrees; rotating the incline during the ascent introduces support motion and possible work on the sphere, so the same distance does not follow.
If 25 degrees describes the final launch configuration after a historical increase from 12 degrees, the answer is 6.08452 m; treating 25 degrees as the angle before the increase gives 4.17669 m.

Outside the rolling regime, surfaces with the same static coefficient q = 0.05 can have different kinetic coefficients, such as 0.01 and 0.04; their sliding decelerations and centre-of-mass stopping distances differ despite identical q.

The outside-regime formula is not determined by the measured static coefficient: during sliding the relevant friction coefficient is kinetic, and the sphere can retain rotation when its centre momentarily stops.

notes: The base answer, stationary-incline equations, radius cancellation and all listed in-regime friction answers are correct. Conditional on completing a prelaunch adjustment from 25 degrees to θ + q, the relevant answers are correctly 4.85249 m, 4.17669 m and 3.77043 m for q = 7, 13 and 18 degrees. That interpretation is not secured for T96D5, and TDEF6 also admits the historical reading recorded in pass 1. The authors' strict friction inequality is sufficient; excluding equality is a harmless boundary convention here. Their outside-regime expression is explicitly a physics claim even though it is excluded from the certified in-regime answers, and it requires an unstated kinetic-friction assumption.
